newsitem.title: USA: U.S. health chief says human cloning "repugnant".
newsitem.headline: U.S. health chief says human cloning "repugnant".

text.p: The chief U.S. scientist on Wednesday condemned any attempt to clone human beings as "poor science and poor ethics" but cautioned that hasty regulation could stifle research beneficial to humanity.

Testifying before a congressional panel, National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Harold Varmus repeatedly and unequivocally dismissed any possible attempt to make a carbon copy of a human being as "morally repugnant."

"This makes interesting movies but poor science and poor ethics," he said. Cloning humans would run counter to the scientific community's fundamental beliefs about humanity, individuality and diversity, he added.

But Varmus said that since a Scottish researcher disclosed on Saturday that he had cloned an adult sheep, people had focused on the most sensational scenarios of human cloning and had not looked at other possible avenues of research.

He distinguished between cloning people and using some aspects of cloning techniques on human cells to understand how genes were turned on and off. Such understanding might lead, for instance, to ways of producing bone marrow for transplants in cancer patients or growing skin tissue for burn victims.
Federal research funds cannot be used for human embryo research, although privately funded laboratories are largely unregulated.

Varmus said he knew of no one trying to clone a person but acknowledged a "renegade" scientist could someday mount such an effort. But he said any legislation to safeguard against that disturbing possibility had to be carefully crafted to ensure good research was not inadvertently discarded too.
"I am concerned about the rush to legislation," he told the House Appropriations subcommittee that controls NIH spending. "We have a new discovery. ... It needs to be absorbed and discussed."
He praised President Bill Clinton for asking a bioethics panel to review these questions over the next three months.

Varmus said animal cloning could help create more productive livestock and may have the potential for producing proteins for use in human medicines, making organs suitable for human transplants and creating animal models for studying human diseases.

He said research could also "open the door to deeper understanding on how genes are turned off and turned on," how, for instance, one cell developed into a liver cell and another became part of the brain, a process called differentiation.

The sheep experiment took a cell that had already differentiated into an udder cell and reprogrammed it to go back to an undifferentiated state in an embryo. "That's a remarkable achievement," Varmus said.
"It has been difficult, if not impossible, to redirect a cell of one type to behave like another type.

"There are some remarkable possibilities here that require exploration and have been fired by the sheep experiments," he said. He listed cancer, burn victims, cystic fibrosis and neuro-degenerative diseases as possibly benefiting from new research paths opened by the sheep experiment.
